sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Through the debate in Parliament, helped Mr Lee and his team get their message across and aid public understanding.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, Mr Lee proposed the NCMP scheme in 1984.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The NCMP scheme made sure that whatever the election outcome, there would always be a certain minimum number at least, of Opposition Members in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Over time, we gradually increased it and we have brought it now to nine.

sections.label: NMP scheme introduced 1990
sections.summary: The 1990 NMP scheme brought civil society voices, so about 20% of Members are not Government Members.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In 1990, we introduced the Nominated Member of Parliament (NMP) scheme to bring into Parliament diverse voices from civil society.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, now if you take elected Opposition Members, NCMPs plus NMPs, altogether about 20% of Members in the House will, at all times, not be Government Members.

sections.label: Opposition parties and NCMP seats
sections.summary: Opposition parties have always taken up NCMP seats offered, except the first time in 1984 when there were special circumstances.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In the last 30 years, other than the very first time in 1984 when there were special circumstances, Opposition parties have always taken up the NCMP seats offered to them.

sections.label: NCMP voting restrictions
sections.summary: NCMPs cannot vote on constitutional changes, supply bills, money bills, votes of no confidence, and removing a President from office.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Unlike constituency Members, NCMPs are restricted in what they can vote on in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: There are a few matters which they cannot vote on: constitutional changes, supply bills, money bills, votes of no confidence, and also removing a President from office.

sections.label: Equal voting rights for NCMPs
sections.summary: The Constitution will be amended to give NCMPs the same voting rights as constituency Members, and the minimum number of Opposition MPs will rise from nine to 12.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But if we accept that NCMPs have as much of a mandate from voters to be in the House as constituency Members of Parliament and more mandate in the House than party list Members of Parliament would in a proportional representation system, then, even in the case of a vote of no confidence and the other restricted matters which NCMPs are presently not allowed to vote on, I think we can make a case and I will make the case that they should not only be allowed to speak, but to vote.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Therefore, I intend to amend the Constitution during this term to give NCMPs the same voting rights as constituency Members of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: NCMPs should therefore be able to vote even in the case of confidence motions, and all the other presently restricted matters.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But there is no reason at all to perceive NCMPs as second-class.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I will also increase the minimum number of Opposition Members of Parliament, including NCMPs, in this House, from the next General Election.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I will increase the number from nine to 12.

sections.label: Group Representation Constituency scheme
sections.summary: The GRC scheme was introduced in 1988 to ensure a minimum number of minority race Members in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Next, let me talk about Group Representation Constituency (GRCs).

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We introduced the GRC scheme in 1988 to ensure that we will always have a minimum number of minority race Members in Parliament.

sections.label: GRC sizes and elected President
sections.summary: The Electoral Boundaries Review Committee will be instructed to reduce average GRC size and create more SMCs; the elected President and Council of Presidential Advisors were created.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The next General Election is a long way off.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I do not want to raise excitement prematurely but I will say now that in due course, when I appoint the Electoral Boundaries Review Committee, I will instruct it to reduce the average size of GRCs further, and to create more SMCs.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In 1990, we passed legislation to make the President an elected office, so that he could act as a stabiliser in our political system.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The President would exercise custodial powers over the spending of past Reserves and key appointments in the public service – the two vital areas which I talked about earlier.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: He would be directly elected by the people in a national election, so as to have the mandate and moral authority to say "no" to the Government, should this become necessary.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We also created a Council of Presidential Advisors (CPA) to assist and advise the President in carrying out his duties and exercising his powers.

sections.label: President's non-executive role
sections.summary: The President has no executive or policymaking role, which remains with the elected Government commanding the majority in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: By design, the President has no executive, policymaking role and this remains the prerogative of the elected Government commanding the majority in Parliament.

sections.label: President's blocking power limits
sections.summary: The Constitution lets the President block certain Government actions in carved-out areas but not initiate or champion policies.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The Constitution gives him power to block certain actions of the Government, in areas which are specifically carved out for him.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But it does not give him the power to initiate policies or generally to champion policies.

sections.label: Constitutional Tribunal and NIRC framework
sections.summary: A Constitutional Tribunal was created for the President to refer constitutional questions, and the NIRC framework was introduced as a spending rule.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We created a Constitutional Tribunal to which the President can refer Constitutional questions which arise for an opinion, especially if there is a disagreement between him and the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We introduced the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) framework, a new spending rule to enable the Government to tap a stable and sustainable income from our Reserves.

sections.label: President's permission for past Reserves
sections.summary: The Government sought the President's permission to use past Reserves to fund the Jobs Credit scheme and Special Risk-Sharing Initiative.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The Government, therefore, sought the President's permission to use past Reserves to fund the Jobs Credit scheme and the Special Risk-Sharing Initiative.

sections.label: Review Elected President qualifying criteria
sections.summary: The passage states that the qualifying criteria for the Elected President should first be reviewed.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: First, we should review the qualifying criteria for the Elected President.

sections.label: Pegging criteria at senior management
sections.summary: The concept was to peg the criteria at people with senior management competence and experience for assessing financial proposals and appointments.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The concept was to peg it at people with senior management competence and experience, because they have to assess and decide on financial proposals which will involve billions of dollars, and they must judge and decide to approve or reject appointments of people into posts which will involve running big organisations, making decisions, investing, managing and spending billions of dollars.

sections.label: Inflation and growing reserves oversight
sections.summary: The passage notes inflation figures and that economic growth, spending, Reserves, and organisation complexity have grown, with the President holding a second key on bodies like MAS, Temasek, GIC, HDB and JTC.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Just based on inflation alone, $100 million in 1990 would be equivalent to $158 million today.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But it is much more than inflation, which is at issue, because over 25 years, our economy has grown, Government spending has gone up, Government Reserves have accumulated, the size and the complexity of the organisations which are subject to the second key of the President have grown many-fold.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Apart from the key appointments in the Government, the President also has a second key on organisations like the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), Temasek Holdings, GIC, the Housing and Development Board (HDB), and JTC.

sections.label: Government Budget spending growth
sections.summary: Government Budget spending rose from S$11 billion in 1990 to S$68 billion in 2015, six times more.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: Our Government spending, the Government Budget, has gone up from S$11 billion in 1990 to S$68 billion in 2015 − six times.

sections.label: Companies with $100 million capital
sections.summary: A report noted about 1,200 registered companies with paid-up capital of $100 million or more in 2010, which the speaker says is 2,100.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: After the last election, he sent me a report and I quote from the report, paragraph 6.1 in the conclusion: "In the course of its work, the Presidential Elections Committee (PEC) noted that there were about 1,200 registered companies with a paid-up capital of $100 million or more in 2010." As I pointed out today, it is 2,100.

sections.label: Reviewing President qualifying criteria
sections.summary: The speaker agrees with Mr Eddie Teo that the qualifying criteria for candidates to be President should be reviewed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: However, the smallest companies in Singapore with a paid-up capital of $100 million today would fall well short in both size and complexity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: This is an issue that the Government may wish to review." I agree with Mr Eddie Teo that we should review the qualifying criteria for candidates to be President.

sections.label: CPA advice weight in decisions
sections.summary: Over time, consideration should be given to whether the CPA's advice should count for more in the President's decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: Over time, as the new institutions of the President and the CPA established themselves, we should consider if the CPA's advice should come to count for more in the decisions made by the President, so as to make our governance system more stable.

sections.label: CPA views in custodial powers
sections.summary: The arrangement does not apply uniformly to the President's custodial powers in other areas, and study is needed on giving the CPA's views greater weight.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: This applies to supply bills, it applies to key appointments, but this arrangement does not apply uniformly when the President exercises custodial powers in other areas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: We should study if the CPA's views should be given greater weight in more areas and, if so, how this can be done.

sections.label: No Malay President since 1991
sections.summary: Since the Elected President system took effect in 1991, there has not been a Malay President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: Since we introduced the Elected President system and brought it into effect in 1991, we have not had a Malay President.

sections.label: Constitutional Commission on Presidency
sections.summary: A Constitutional Commission chaired by Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon will study eligibility criteria, the CPA and periodic minority Presidents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: It is the same problem with Parliamentary Elections which led us to create GRCs to ensure a minimum representation of minority race Members in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: I think we should consider a similar mechanism for Presidential Elections to ensure that minorities can be periodically elected if we have not had a particular minority as President for some time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: These are three broad areas to look into: (a) to bring the eligibility criteria up to date; (b) to strengthen the CPA; and (c) to ensure minority Presidents periodically.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: I will appoint a Constitutional Commission to study these issues and make recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: It will be chaired by Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon and include distinguished jurists, academics and corporate executives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: The Commission will look into each of these issues, take views from the public and, in due course, it will recommend how we can improve the system – I hope by the third quarter of this year.

sections.label: National Day Parade reserve commander
sections.summary: The speaker was at the Padang as reserve commander for the PCF Marching Contingent of the National Day Parade.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: That way, future Governments can work with future citizens of Singapore to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for our people.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: I was at the Padang as I had the privilege to be the reserve commander for the PCF Marching Contingent of the National Day Parade (NDP).

sections.label: Punggol-Damai SG50 celebration
sections.summary: The speaker rushed to his constituency for a Punggol-Damai Residents' Committee SG50 celebration attended by several hundred families.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: When I left the Padang later that evening, I had an extra spring in my step and a song in my heart.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: I was rushing back to my constituency to join the Punggol-Damai Residents' Committee for an SG50 celebration.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: They had worked very hard for many weeks, decorating their estate, building a little kampong, putting up flags everywhere, some big, some small.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: It was a great event, a huge event, with several hundred families having a great time.

sections.label: Last song Majulah Singapura
sections.summary: The last song was going to be "Majulah Singapura".

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: The last song, of course, was going to be "Majulah Singapura".

sections.label: Boy singing out of time
sections.summary: A young voice sang loudly and with gusto but out of time during the pause between the verses.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Even worse, he did not know the timing.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: So, as the first verse finished with "Berjaya Singapura", there is that pause into the short silence between the verses, you could hear this young voice with all his energy and gusto trying to sing, and trying loudly to sing but you could not really hear the words he was singing – completely out of time.

sections.label: Race not asked about story
sections.summary: The speaker says no one has asked about the race of the boys in his story, which is about Singaporeans regardless of race, language or religion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: In the Singapore of today, and in the six months I have been telling the story and boring my grassroots leaders with it, I have never even once been asked about the race of these boys – the soldiers and the little boy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: What does that say about the Singapore of today, that when I tell a story like this, it does not occur to anyone to ask, because it does not change the story – the story is about Singapore and Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion.

sections.label: New citizen among boys
sections.summary: The passage asks what happens if one of the boys in the story is a new citizen.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: And listening to my story, you understand this, you believe this, you embrace this.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: But what if one of those boys is a new citizen?

sections.label: Meaning of race language religion
sections.summary: The passage asks what the phrase regardless of race, language or religion means.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: What does it mean "Regardless of race, language or religion"?

sections.label: Deeds words over Constitution pledge
sections.summary: The passage states that dealing with fault lines of division depends less on the Constitution or pledge and more on deeds, actions and words.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: How we deal with fault lines of division, depends less on the Constitution or our pledge and more on our deeds, our actions and our words – words that are said, words that are held back.

sections.label: No second-class citizens
sections.summary: The passage states the idea that there would be no second-class citizens and no child should grow up believing they are one.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: The idea that in our country, there would be no second-class citizens.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: No child in Singapore should grow up believing that they are a second-class citizen.

sections.label: Religiously diverse racial harmony integration
sections.summary: The passage states that after 50 years Singapore is one of the most religiously diverse countries, with celebrated racial harmony and integration.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: After a short 50 years, we are one of the most religiously diverse countries in the world, and our racial harmony and integration are celebrated and something to be rightly proud of.

sections.label: Deeds words for unity harmony
sections.summary: The passage states that building a Singapore with unity of purpose depends most on deeds and words, spoken and held back.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: If we are to build a Singapore with a unity of purpose, a nation that sees our diversity as strength, then it is our deeds and our words, spoken and held back that will matter most.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: We are a people who want unity and harmony and are prepared to put in the hard work to make this happen.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: We are a people who understand that our diversity is our strength.

sections.label: SkillsFuture and future skills
sections.summary: SkillsFuture will prepare Singapore for the future economy through re-skilling, up-skilling, second-skilling, deep-skilling and multi-skilling.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: SkillsFuture will help to prepare us for the future economy through various skills, be it re-skilling, up-skilling, second-skilling, deep-skilling and even multi-skilling.

sections.label: Entrepreneur schemes and SkillsFuture
sections.summary: Government entrepreneur schemes exist, and SkillsFuture Credit and Earn and Learn can sharpen entrepreneurship and other career skills to enhance income and employment.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Presently, there are many assistance schemes for entrepreneurs by the Government, like the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC), iSTART Accelerate and Catalyse Entrepreneurship (iSTART: ACE), and Capability Development Grant (CDG), among others.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: At the same time, the SkillsFuture initiatve – for instance, the SkillsFuture Credit and the SkillsFuture Earn and Learn – can help to improve and sharpen our skills in entrepreneurship as well as in other careers, with the aim of enhancing the income and employment opportunities for Singaporeans.

sections.label: Undergraduates in general degree programmes
sections.summary: The speaker urges MOE to help general degree undergraduates gain cross-discipline attachments, internships, multi-skilling or second-skilling for future employability.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, at the same time, I am also concerned about one specific group of Singaporeans – our university undergraduates, particularly those in general degree programmes, who may not have industry-relevant training or skills.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I would urge the MOE to look at how students in such programmes can benefit from cross-discipline attachments or internships, and opportunities for multi-skilling or second-skilling during the course of their undergraduate studies, so that they are more employable in future.

sections.label: Reviewing academic stream categorisation
sections.summary: The speaker urges MOE to review how students are categorised into Express, Normal (Academic) or Normal (Technical) streams.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Specifically, I would urge MOE to review the way we categorise our students in schools into academic streams – Express or Normal (Academic) or Normal (Technical).

sections.label: CCE lessons and SAP school admission
sections.summary: The speaker proposes teaching CCE in common or form classes instead of Mother Tongue, and opening SAP schools to non-Chinese Mother Tongue students who take Chinese as a third language.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: First, in teaching Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) in schools, I propose that this be changed from being taught in Mother Tongue classes to common lessons or in the form classes at the primary school level.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The rationale for teaching CCE in Mother Tongue classes may be to address racial issues or values more sensitively, but I believe that after 50 years of nation-building, our society is mature enough and sensible enough to discuss sensitive issues pertaining to character or citizenship openly and honestly, starting with our children who are even more race-blind.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Second, I would like to once again propose that our Special Assistance Plan (SAP) schools be opened up to admit students who do not take Chinese as a Mother Tongue language but who meet the school's cut-off point for the PSLE.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I would propose that as a requirement of admission, these students will have to take Chinese as a third language from Secondary 1 to Secondary 4.

sections.label: Piloting enhanced SAP schools
sections.summary: The speaker asks for SAP schools to be enhanced and their social environment enriched, and for MOE to pilot this in one or two SAP schools.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I am asking for the SAP schools to be enhanced and for its social environment to be enriched.

sentences.speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I am asking for MOE to pilot this in one or two SAP schools to see how it works out.

sections.label: Urban landscape transformations
sections.summary: This passage states transformations to the urban landscape, including changing land use, raising plot ratios at transport hubs, and building future economy clusters.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: This may entail the following transformations to our urban landscape.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We need to facilitate the change of land use and increase plot ratio for residential developments at key transport hubs.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We need to provide more incentives for businesses to move into future economy clusters.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: This involves relocating existing supporting businesses and building new business clusters for future economy industries including smart city technologies, medical and pharmaceutical manufacturing or finance and professional services.

sections.label: Planning unit for HDB towns
sections.summary: This passage states that a planning unit is needed to develop infrastructure connectivity master plans for all HDB towns.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: To achieve this, we need to set up a planning unit to develop infrastructure connectivity master plans for all HDB towns.

sections.label: Flats above 40 storeys
sections.summary: This passage states that MND and HDB can explore building flats above 40 storeys and replacing car parks with basement car parks.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In this regard, the Ministry of National Development (MND) and the HDB can explore innovative solutions to build flats above 40 storeys and replace surface and multi-storey car parks with basement car parks.

sections.label: Public transport connectivity and passes
sections.summary: This passage states that better express bus and train connectivity will encourage public transport use, and proposes a weekend day pass priced at $2.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Better connectivity of express buses and trains from residential clusters to business districts, shopping areas or the airport will encourage more people to take public transport.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We can also introduce weekend public transport day pass at an attractive price such as $2 for multiple trips.

sections.label: Green Mark Building Scheme incentives
sections.summary: This passage proposes that BCA step up the Green Mark Building Scheme and give more incentives for buildings to go green or become zero-energy.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: As Singapore's economy moves up the value chain, there will be more people working in indoor air-conditioned work environments, such as offices and laboratories.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: I propose that the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) step up the Green Mark Building Scheme and provide more incentives for all buildings to go green or become zero-energy buildings.

sections.label: Green Mark for homes
sections.summary: This passage states that BCA can consider setting up a Green Mark for homes and providing incentives for homeowners to make homes eco-friendly and sustainable.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: BCA can consider setting up a Green Mark for homes and provide incentives for homeowners to make their homes eco-friendly and sustainable.

sections.label: HDB block camera installations
sections.summary: Over 52,000 cameras have been installed in 8,600 HDB blocks to date.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: To date, over 52,000 cameras have been installed in 8,600 HDB blocks.

sections.label: Lift telemonitoring response time
sections.summary: The lift telemonitoring system at HDB blocks lets lift technicians respond within 25 minutes to rescue trapped passengers.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: For example, the lift telemonitoring system at HDB blocks allows our lift technicians to respond within 25 minutes to rescue trapped passengers in lifts.

sections.label: Building a vertical city
sections.summary: With limited land for development in Singapore, building a vertical city should be considered.

sentences.speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: With limited land for development in Singapore, we should start to consider building a vertical city which will allow Singaporeans to live their lives with greatest enjoyment.

sections.label: Unwed mothers' scheme entitlements
sections.summary: Unwed mothers get half the maternity leave, no Baby Bonus or Parenthood Tax Rebates, and limited housing access.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Unwed mothers have half the maternity leave entitlements, do not get perks such as the Baby Bonus cash gift and the Parenthood Tax Rebates.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: They cannot have access to BTO flats or the ASSIST housing scheme and must also wait until they are 35 years old to buy a flat under the singles scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: They are currently marginalised under our schemes, and more could be done to assist them in their time of need, especially if there are little or no grounds to differentiate them from other mothers.

sections.label: Senior workers' re-employment treatment
sections.summary: Senior workers with similar output may receive less in employer CPF contributions or reduced benefits and wages at re-employment.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Senior workers who put in the same amount of effort and time at work as everyone else, generating similar output, but receive less in their employer's CPF contributions or have their benefits and wages reduced at the point of re-employment.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We should do more to change the mindsets of employers and colleagues, and to enable and motivate companies to restructure their workplace to enhance the productivity of our senior workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We can do more to entrench a fair and just re-employment framework, continue to narrow the gap of their employer's CPF contribution so as to enable them to embrace a productive and fulfilling ageing.

sections.label: NS deferment for elite sportsmen
sections.summary: Only two young men have obtained deferment, and a wider net is sought for elite sportsmen.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Right now, only two young men have obtained deferment – Joseph Schooling, at 21 this year, and probably in good stead for another two more Olympics; and Quah Ting Wen, at 19, is another.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We need to cast a wider net to find promising individuals and team sportsmen who can potentially win medals for Singapore, not just at the Olympics, but also the Asian Games.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Can we have an NS Scheme for our elite sportsmen that allows these elite athletes in their prime to bring glory to Singapore on the world stage and serve their NS obligations later?

sections.label: WHO mental health definition
sections.summary: WHO defines mental health as a state of well-being, not just absence of mental disorder, and estimated 450 million people have a mental problem.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Mental health as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) refers to "a state of well-being" and "not just the absence of mental disorder".

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It was previously estimated by WHO that about 450 million people have a mental problem.

sections.label: Mental health awareness and resources
sections.summary: More awareness and understanding are needed for an emotionally resilient society, and increased resource allocation for services and infrastructure to meet Singapore's mental health needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We need to address this with more mental health awareness and understanding to build an emotionally resilient and supportive society.

sentences.speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: There is a need for increased resource allocation to continue the development of services and infrastructure to ensure that we have sufficient capacity and capability to cater to the increasing mental health needs in Singapore.

sections.label: Ageing population and economy
sections.summary: Singapore faces an ageing population and declining workforce, requiring economic restructuring, with the Committee on the Future Economy critical for competitiveness and good jobs.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: In this next chapter of our Singapore story, we are faced with a strategic challenge of an ageing population and a declining workforce.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: We need to recognise this impending change that is already at our doorstep and restructure our economy to adapt and sustain growth.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: The work of the Committee on the Future Economy will be critical to ensure that our economy can remain competitive and Singaporeans can continue to aspire to good jobs and opportunities.

sections.label: Evolving meritocracy and opportunities
sections.summary: Everyone should discover and develop strengths and contribute meaningfully, evolving meritocracy toward broader success while giving children equal access to school opportunities.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: We must provide the opportunity for everyone to discover their strengths, develop them and then contribute to society in meaningful ways.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: This is the direction in which we must continue to evolve our approach to meritocracy, so that our system encompasses broader definitions of success and fulfilment.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: While we cannot ensure equal outcomes, we should provide children equal access to opportunities in our schools.

sections.label: Forget Us Not dementia initiative
sections.summary: The Lien Foundation and Khoo Teck Puat Hospital initiative in Yishun Chong Pang raises dementia awareness, training Citizens-on-Patrol residents and over 6,000 people and businesses.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: I recently saw a video of "Forget Us Not", which is an independent initiative organised by the Lien Foundation and Khoo Teck Puat Hospital.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: This initiative was kick-started in Yishun Chong Pang area to raise awareness of the growing number of persons with dementia.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: This is perhaps a tribute to our ageing population.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: It involves the Neighbourhood Police Centre and 80 Citizens-on-Patrol residents trained to detect, respond and assist persons with dementia whom they may meet during patrols.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: The initiative also organised education talks on dementia and conducted training sessions to over 6,000 people and businesses.

sections.label: The Hidden Good movement
sections.summary: Because good acts can go unnoticed and people get cynical about the Singapore Heartbeat, two then-NSFs, Leon and Rovik, started The Hidden Good in 2013.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: But sometimes, such acts can go unnoticed amongst us and that is why, sometimes, people get cynical about the Singapore Heartbeat.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: This inspired a movement called The Hidden Good, started by two then-NSFs, Leon and Rovik, back in 2013 when I was still in the SAF.

sections.label: Youth movement and Singapore Heartbeat
sections.summary: A youth movement on social media highlights simple good deeds, bringing forth the Singapore Heartbeat.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: It could be simple things like someone giving up their seat on the MRT or someone helping a "popo" to reach the groceries on the top shelf in a supermarket.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: This youth movement has gained a lot of traction on social media, bringing to light the "hidden good" of society, bringing forth the Singapore Heartbeat.

sections.label: Growing economy, defence, Singapore heart
sections.summary: The speaker calls for growing the economy, defending the country and forging a strong Singapore heart.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: We must continue to think wisely with our head to grow our economy.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: We must build our muscle to defend our country.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: At the same time, I call on this House and fellow Singaporeans to forge a strong Singapore heart.

sentences.speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
sentences.text: As long as our Singapore heart beats strong and steady, as long as we remain united as one people, I am optimistic and confident that we will build an exceptional and enduring Singapore for our children and our children's children.

sections.label: SkillsFuture and confident Singaporeans
sections.summary: Nurturing confident Singaporeans is the way to ensure children and grandchildren thrive, and SkillsFuture contains the DNA for this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Hence, nurturing a confident Singaporean people is the way to ensure that our children and grandchildren will thrive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I believe the Government's SkillsFuture programme contains the DNA for empowering confident Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, it is all-inclusive and does not discriminate on the basis of household background, income and employment status, educational attainment or age.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Second, it trusts individual Singaporeans to be the ones who know themselves best and have the wisdom to know where they should head to next in life.

sections.label: SkillsFuture credit empowering Singaporeans
sections.summary: The $500 SkillsFuture credit is not big, but the policy focuses on empowering Singaporeans rather than directing them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Although the $500 SkillsFuture credit is not a big sum, many people are exploring ways to use the credit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Fifth, and most importantly, the whole policy is focused on empowering Singaporeans, instead of trying to direct or steer them to fit into the planned economy or the needs of corporations.

sections.label: Defining national interest by consensus
sections.summary: National interest should be defined by consensus and the narrative should not be monopolised by the ruling party.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: National interest should be defined by consensus and the narrative should not be shaped and monopolised by the ruling party.

sections.label: Building independent institutions
sections.summary: The Government and ruling party must let go and allow independent institutions trusted by the people to be built.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government and the ruling party must be able to let go and allow the building of independent institutions trusted by the people, regardless of race, language, religion and political affiliation.

sections.label: Value of alternative parties
sections.summary: The passage argues alternative parties are valuable as insurance against ruling party collapse and calls for a system conducive to their growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Excessive fears of political gridlock will lead to a society depending only on one political party, waiting for it to rot to the point of no return before any alternative party can be formed to take its place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We must see value in having alternative parties around and having the opportunities to develop.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Alternative parties are valuable because they are an insurance against any collapse or failure of the existing ruling party.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If this Government truly believes in preserving this shining red dot, then the onus is on it to build a political system conducive to the growth of alternative parties as well as the renewal of the ruling party.

sections.label: Shared Values White Paper debate
sections.summary: The House debated and passed a White Paper on Shared Values in 1991 after a two-day debate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Members of this House had, over the past days, alluded to some of these, such as the generosity of spirit, resilience, valuing racial and religious harmony, meritocracy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: This House had, in fact, debated on a White Paper on Shared Values in 1991 and passed it after a two-day debate.

sections.label: Sense of responsibility value
sections.summary: The speaker believes a sense of responsibility, for both Government and citizens, should prevail in the next half century.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In this regard, I believe there is another value that should prevail as we chart our way into the next half century, that is, the sense of responsibility – both on the part of the Government as well as on the part of the Singapore citizen.

sections.label: Financial assistance income checks
sections.summary: Financial assistance applications involve checks on the income and contributions of children or other family members.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: For example, when one makes an application for financial assistance, checks are made on the income and contributions of his or her children or other family members.

sections.label: Support stops before stability
sections.summary: Support is often available only until employment and means test are met, though some families still struggle after assistance stops.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Another aspect of this I would like to highlight is that the support for the individual or family is often only available till they are able to find employment and meet the means test.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: However, in some of these cases, the families are still struggling for a while after assistance has stopped.

sections.label: Bilahari Kausikan on adapting
sections.summary: Bilahari Kausikan said the world constantly changes and will not change to suit our conveniences, so we must adapt.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Ambassador-at-Large, Mr Bilahari Kausikan, in his speech during the Singapore Perspectives Conference in January 2015, said: "The world is constantly changing and since the world will not change to suit our conveniences, we will have to constantly adapt to it.

sections.label: NCMPs and diversity of views
sections.summary: The speaker welcomes the Prime Minister's announcements to increase NCMP numbers and extend their powers as steps toward diversity of views in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, how do we make it our strength and not cause our fall?

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I feel that the Prime Minister's announcements yesterday regarding increasing the number of Non-Constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs) in Parliament and extending powers of NCMPs, are concrete steps towards bringing diversity of views in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I, therefore, welcome this proposal as it allows for respectful discourse on real issues that matter to Singaporeans and leads to the shaping of useful and important policies for the people.

sections.label: Muslim community Islamophobia concern
sections.summary: The Muslim community has expressed concern over increasing Islamophobia and some Muslims growing more distant from the rest of the Singaporean community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: The Muslim community has expressed concern over the increasing Islamophobia and the observation that some Muslims are growing somewhat more distant from the rest of the Singaporean community.

sections.label: Racial and religious harmony discussions
sections.summary: The speaker says racial and religious harmony efforts should go beyond attending cultural events and allow space to discuss identities and religious practices.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Our efforts in encouraging racial and religious harmony can no longer be at a superficial level of attending each other's cultural events.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: We should allow for space to talk about our identities, our religious practices, such as the burning of incense paper, the wearing of the tudung, the playing of music during Thaipusam, for example.

sections.label: Community loyalty not questioned
sections.summary: The speaker says the community cannot be blamed and its loyalty should not be questioned.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Surely, our community cannot be blamed and our loyalty should not be questioned.

sections.label: Tudung issue on community's minds
sections.summary: The speaker says the tudung issue is constantly in the minds of the community.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: One other thing that is constantly in the minds of our community is the tudung issue.

sections.label: Constitutional changes by Prime Minister Lee
sections.summary: Prime Minister Lee spoke about changes to the Constitution of Singapore, including smaller GRCs and changes to Elected President eligibility criteria.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Prime Minister Lee yesterday spoke about the changes to the Constitution of Singapore, including having smaller GRCs and the changes to the eligibility criteria for the Elected President.

sections.label: Elected President minority eligibility
sections.summary: PM Lee said a process will ensure minorities are not excluded and there will be a minority President, though the speaker wants Malays chosen for merit.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: In changing the eligibility criteria for the Elected President, Prime Minister Lee said that there will be a process to ensure that minorities will not be excluded and there will be a President from the minority group.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: We would definitely like to see representation from our community but we would like our Malays to be chosen because he or she is the best and not because of his or her race.

sections.label: NCMP scheme improvements
sections.summary: The speaker welcomes the improvements to the NCMP scheme.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: As I have mentioned earlier, I welcome the improvements to the NCMP scheme.

sections.label: SkillsFuture for lifelong learning
sections.summary: The Government implemented measures including SkillsFuture to prepare students and workforce and support lifelong learning.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: The Government has implemented several measures to prepare our students and workforce, one of which is SkillsFuture, to support lifelong learning.

sections.label: SkillsFuture urgency for workers
sections.summary: People like Adam may struggle to find time for SkillsFuture, and untrained workers will be most affected, so its urgency must be stressed.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: People like Adam who needs SkillsFuture the most may have difficulties finding time for it.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: We need to stress the urgency and importance of SkillsFuture for the current generation of workers because, like Adam, they have not been trained in new technologies and they will be the ones who will be most affected.

sections.label: Job redundancy productivity question
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether making 30% to 40% of jobs redundant would bring higher productivity, higher unemployment, or both.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: If about 30% to 40% of our jobs were to be made redundant, will we achieve higher productivity, higher unemployment, or both?

sections.label: National plan on ageing
sections.summary: The Ministerial Committee on Ageing announced a $3 billion national plan to help Singaporeans age confidently and lead active lives.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: Last year, the Ministerial Committee on Ageing announced a $3 billion national plan to help Singaporeans age confidently and lead active lives.

sections.label: Inter-generational facilities for elders
sections.summary: As elders grow in number, the speaker proposes accelerating development of inter-generational facilities benefiting young and old.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: As the number of elders in our society grows, I would like to propose that we accelerate the Page: 43 development of these inter-generational facilities that will benefit both the young and the old.

sections.label: Grandparents, parks and childcare centres
sections.summary: Facilities would let grandparents who send grandchildren to school stay on, mingle or join eldercare programmes, and neighbourhood parks could host childcare centres.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: Like Mdm Tan's family, many of our young are cared for by their grandparents while their parents work.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: These facilities will provide a nexus for these grandparents who send their grandchildren to school, to stay on, mingle, get involved as a volunteer or even be a participant in the eldercare programmes.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: The second public facility that can be better used is our many beautiful neighbourhood parks.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: I recently learnt that this idea will be implemented in Tokyo, with three wards in Tokyo opening childcare centres in urban parks next year.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: Locations, such as Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park and Tampines Sun Plaza Park, would be suitable.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: These parks are close to HDB heartlands, have convenient drop-off and pick-up points and ample space.

sections.label: Multi-generational neighbourhoods vision
sections.summary: The speaker hopes for multi-generational neighbourhoods where elderly and young mingle and share lives and experiences.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: What do we hope to see when we reach that age?

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: I hope that we will be a nation of multi-generational neighbourhoods, where we take care of each other and where our elderly and our young can mingle and share their lives and experiences, like Mdm Tan and her granddaughter.

sections.label: Fostering a caring society
sections.summary: The speaker calls fostering a caring society the most critical of five interdependent aims, focusing on caring for elderly and young families.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: In fact, I believe these five aims are interdependent and, for me, the most critical of these aims would be the need to foster a caring society, one in which our people feel meaningfully engaged and are actively involved.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Therefore, please allow me to speak on the aim of fostering a more caring society and, more specifically, on how we can all care more for our elderly and young families.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: We must care for our elderly, make sure that their needs are catered for, so that they need not live in anxiety and fear post-retirement, or worse, gloomily count down to the last day of their lives.

sections.label: Ageing in place and technology
sections.summary: The speaker says continued investment in technological research and expedited implementation of tested solutions can enable elderly to live independently at home.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Moreover, this does not align well with our vision of "ageing in place".

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Therefore, we must continue to invest in technological research and expedite the implementation of tested solutions that can enable our elderly to live independently at home.

sections.label: Ageing workforce and age discrimination
sections.summary: With an ageing population and rising average workforce age, enabling elderly to stay and thrive in jobs is a social responsibility and economic imperative, and age discrimination at recruitment must be stemmed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Thirdly, as we have an ageing population, the average age of our workforce is expected to rise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Hence, it is not just a social responsibility to enable our elderly to stay and, indeed, to thrive in their jobs, but there is economic imperative as well, given the tight labour market.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Age discrimination at work, especially at the point of recruitment, must be stemmed out.

sections.label: Care, respect, cherish elderly
sections.summary: The speaker hopes to end prejudices against age and proposes advocating care for, respect for and cherishing of the elderly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: I hope we can end these prejudices and take action to help everyone recognise that age should not be a barrier, that an elderly can still be driven, useful and healthy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Hence, I propose that we should advocate three ideas: care for the elderly, respect the elderly and cherish the elderly.

sections.label: Elderly living alone at home
sections.summary: The speaker says most elderly prefer to spend their last days at home and urges redesigning homes and using assistive technologies.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Although we are building more nursing homes to meet the needs of an ageing society, most elderly prefer to spend their last days in their own home, not a nursing home or a home for the elderly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: In addition, there is a rising trend of elderly living alone, so we should help them – indeed, for ourselves in future, too – redesign their homes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: We should use technology and actively research and implement assistive technologies, so that the elderly who live alone or have disabilities can lead a safer and more independent life.

sections.label: Support for raising young
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether parents can raise their young without compromising aspirational pursuits, welcoming more infant, childcare and student care centres.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Can we not better enable them to raise their young whilst not having to compromise on their aspirational pursuits?

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: I am glad that the Government is increasing the supply of infant care, childcare and student care centres, as well as proactively strengthening the quality of such centre-based care.

sections.label: Network of housewives
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether a formal network of housewives within communities could be systematically identified and built up.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Could we systematically identify and build up a formal network of housewives within communities?

sections.label: Married Child Priority Scheme quota
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the quota of flats under the Married Child Priority Scheme per BTO development could be increased.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Two, could we further facilitate familial support by increasing the quota of flats set aside under the Married Child Priority Scheme (MCPS) per BTO development?

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: The Government must be credited for enhancing MCPS about two years ago and for introducing the Proximity Housing Grant (PHG) last year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: This challenge is exacerbated when their parents live in mature estates, where flat supply is already scarce and where competition is also keener.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Hence, while the PHG helps to offset part of a resale flat's price premium over a subsidised one, it is still not enough to make a resale flat within the affordability range to them.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: As such, could we seriously consider Page: 47 increasing the quota of flats set aside under MCPS per BTO development?

sections.label: Flexi-work for mothers
sections.summary: The speaker questions whether remarks were necessary and says more flexi-work arrangements are needed so mothers can contribute fully.

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: Her employer approved of the leave anyway because it was mandated, but were the remarks necessary?

sentences.speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
sentences.text: We need to enable more flexi-work arrangements so that mothers can still contribute fully even as they take childcare leave.

sections.label: Good politics for good policies
sections.summary: The Prime Minister said yesterday that good politics is needed to make good policies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: As the Prime Minister said yesterday, we need good politics to make for good policies.

sections.label: Group Representation Constituency scheme example
sections.summary: The passage cites the Group Representation Constituency scheme as an instance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Take the Group Representation Constituency (GRC) scheme, for instance.

sections.label: Obama on Singapore unity
sections.summary: In June 2015, President Obama said Singapore succeeded partly by bringing together people who look different but think of themselves as Singaporean.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In June 2015, US President Barack Obama observed this about Singapore in a dialogue with young Asian leaders and he said: "And the truth of the matter is that one of the reasons that Singapore, as I mentioned earlier, has been successful, is that it has been able to bring together people who may look different, but they all think of themselves as part of Singapore.

sections.label: Bumiputera-only mall opened
sections.summary: Instead of bridging the divide, a bumiputera-only mall was designated and opened in December 2015 with free six months' rental to Malay entrepreneurs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Instead of seeking to bridge the divide, they decided to designate a "bumiputera-only" mall in response; that opened in December 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In fact, it came with free six months' rental to Malay entrepreneurs.

sections.label: GRC system prevents racial politics
sections.summary: The GRC system, implemented in 1988, prevents racial polarisation in politics and guarantees minority representation in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The GRC system was implemented in 1988 precisely to prevent politics in Singapore from being polarised along racial lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Aside from guaranteeing minority representation in Parliament, the requirement that at least one candidate of each GRC belongs to a minority community means Page: 50 that candidates and their political parties cannot campaign on racial lines.

sections.label: Retaining and enhancing Elected Presidency
sections.summary: The passage says it is now more important than ever to retain and enhance the Elected Presidency, citing foreign reserves and GDP per capita growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Far from heeding the calls to abolish the Elected Presidency, I think it is now even more important than ever that we retain and enhance it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: We have heard from the Prime Minister yesterday that our foreign reserves have grown almost 10 times in the period 1988 to 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Our GDP per capita has grown about eight times in that same period.

sections.label: Paid-up threshold review
sections.summary: The paid-up threshold has become obsolete and should be reviewed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: First, obviously, the paid-up threshold has become obsolete and that should be reviewed.

sections.label: Enhancing CPA advisers
sections.summary: The CPA should have more than six advisers, drawn from diverse fields and civil society, who outline their grounds of advice except on national security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: First, to have more than just the current six members available as advisers to the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The CPA should be enhanced with competent experts appointed from across a diverse range of fields as well as from across a spectrum of civil society who, collectively, can represent a broad cross-section of stakeholders in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Second, I would also suggest that these advisers be required to outline the grounds on which they give their advice, save on matters of national security.

sections.label: Revised NCMP scheme aims
sections.summary: The revised NCMP scheme seeks to enhance, enlarge and make the scheme more robust, giving the Opposition an expanded voice in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: That is precisely what the NCMP scheme, as now currently revised, seeks to achieve.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It will be enhanced, it will be enlarged, it will be made more robust and it will give the Opposition an expanded voice in Parliament.

sections.label: NCMP second chance
sections.summary: The NCMP scheme gives the Opposition a second chance, offering best losers a seat with parliamentary privileges of an elected Member.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But if you do not, then the NCMP scheme still gives the Opposition a second chance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Hence, in cases where the Opposition candidate has tried but failed to win the mandate of the people, then, in those cases, the best losers are, nonetheless, offered a seat in Parliament – now with all the parliamentary privileges of an elected Member.

sections.label: NCMP versus elected Member
sections.summary: A former NCMP says NCMPs contribute to debates but it can never be the same as being an elected Member representing constituents.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Because from what I understood from what Mr Low said, basically, he was making the point that they are not the same.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And speaking for myself as a former NCMP, I can say definitively that while yes, we are in the Chamber to contribute to debates, but it can never be the same as being an elected Member representing constituents.

sections.label: Expanded NCMP voting rights
sections.summary: The expanded scheme gives NCMPs greater voices in numbers and, under the Prime Minister's amendments, voting on an equal footing with elected Members.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: The fact of the matter is that the scheme being expanded Page: 53 gives the NCMP greater voices in Parliament in terms of numbers, at least, and also with the proposed amendments by the Prime Minister, they are now voting on an equal footing with elected Members.

sections.label: NCMPs ground presence
sections.summary: Nothing in the current scheme prevents NCMPs from being visible, present and active on the ground.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: If you choose to be proactive on the ground, you can be present well beyond what the current NCMPs might well be doing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: But the fact of the matter is, nothing in the scheme today precludes the NCMP from being visible, present and active on the ground.

sections.label: Ageing population numbers
sections.summary: About 300,000 citizens are above 65, and the number will triple to 900,000 or more by 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: All of us know that we have an ageing population, brought about by ever-improving longevity and prolonged low birth rates.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: We are told that we have, by a recent count ,some 300,000 citizens above the age of 65 and that by the sheer movement of the baby boomers through time, that the number will triple to 900,000 or more by the year 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: And, of course, if we were to count from those aged 50 and above, the numbers would be even bigger.

sections.label: Health of mature Singaporeans
sections.summary: Mature Singaporeans today are on the whole in better physical shape than equivalent-age citizens two or three decades ago.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: If this growing segment is strong, healthy and capable, then we have an advantage nationally.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: If it is weak, sickly and outdated, we will have to find more resources in order to pay for its upkeep.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: If we look around us − and for those of us, middle-aged, you just look at our cohorts − I think it is fair to say that, by way of physical health, mature Singaporeans today at whatever chronological age are, on the whole, in a better shape than those of equivalent-age citizens two or three decades ago.

sections.label: Flat 2015 local jobs growth
sections.summary: MOM's Employment Report shows net local jobs growth for 2015 has basically become flat after more robust growth previously.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: MOM released today an Employment Report showing that net local jobs growth in the economy for 2015 has basically become flat, following more robust growth previously.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: So, it is continuing with its efforts to promote quality growth, to get quality jobs for locals, to maintain and strengthen the Singaporean Core, even as our economy and the local labour supply do not grow like before.

sections.label: Using older workforce
sections.summary: The older segment of the workforce is growing and should be made best use of, as the overall workforce will peak between 2020 and 2025.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: In short, we have to make the best use of every single person.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: And if a segment in that workforce, namely, the older segment, is growing, then you want to make the best use of that certainly, especially when we are told by previous reports by MOM, by the National Population and Talent Division (NPTD) that this workforce will, in fact, peak, on an overall basis, sometime between 2020 and 2025.

sections.label: Re-employment age ceiling raise
sections.summary: 85% of unionised companies employ workers beyond 65, and tripartite partners are finalising raising the re-employment age ceiling from 65 to 67.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: As of December last year, through surveys done by the NTUC, 85% of unionised companies are consciously employing workers beyond the age of 65.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: Tripartite partners are finalising the implementation schedule of raising the re-employment age ceiling from 65 to 67 and I am confident that the agreement will be made public soon.

sections.label: Age limit raised to 75
sections.summary: In December last year the Government raised the age limit from 70 to 75, subject to the motorist passing specified medical and driving proficiency tests.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: And I was glad that the Government heeded the needs of groups of Singaporeans in that kind of situation and updated the policy.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: So, in December last year, it raised the age limit from 70 to 75, subject to the motorist passing specified medical and driving proficiency tests.

sections.label: CPF and retirement support measures
sections.summary: The passage lists CPF and retirement measures including higher salary ceilings, SRS cap, contribution rates for older workers, CPF LIFE and Silver Support.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: From the CPF angle, higher CPF salary ceilings, higher Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS) contribution cap; raising CPF contribution rates for older workers, equalising those aged 50 to 55 with younger workers; enhancing progressivity through extra CPF interest.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: The CPF LIFE scheme would also pay CPF members a stream of income in old age, with the Silver Support Scheme providing additional support for low-income seniors.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: CPF contribution rate ceilings, differences and interest rates should, of course, be periodically reviewed to ensure that they keep in step with changes in, for example, nominal income, as well as changes in conditions of the labour and money markets.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: It is still common to hear the phrase "Asset Rich Cash Poor".

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
sentences.text: Hence, the Government should also examine the experience of facilitating the monetisation of property assets in retirement.

sections.label: 2015 manpower and employment data
sections.summary: MOM released 2015 manpower and employment data showing employment growth down and lowest in 13 years, with unemployment flat.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Just this morning, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) released a set of manpower and employment data for 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Employment growth in 2015 is down and the lowest in 13 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Unemployment is flat but we must not assume it will stay flat or low.

sections.label: Fair Consideration Framework and Jobs Bank
sections.summary: The Fair Consideration Framework and National Jobs Bank had been rolled out in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The Fair Consideration Framework and National Jobs Bank had been rolled out in 2014.

sections.label: Employment data and IT sector feedback
sections.summary: The employment data released that morning seemed to have confirmed ground feedback about the IT sector.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The employment data fleshed out this morning seemed to have confirmed the ground feedback about the IT sector.

sections.label: PME dependency ratio and EP conditions
sections.summary: Two proposals: impose a PME dependency ratio for problem sectors, and stricter Employment Pass conditions for companies with the two weaks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The first is to impose a PME dependency ratio, similar to that for Work Permits and S Passes, for problem sectors which display the two "weaks" – weak Singaporean Core and a weak commitment to hire and develop Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The second is to impose stricter Employment Pass application conditions and requirements for companies with the two "weaks".

sections.label: Retrenchment and Singaporean PMEs
